why_use_this:
Reach for this package when you need to manipulate a mathematical expression AS an expression -- differentiate it symbolically, simplify it, substitute values and evaluate it, print it back out -- rather than just computing a single numeric answer. This is what distinguishes it from every other numeric package in the ecosystem: [vani-calculus](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-calculus)'s `diff_central` gives you a NUMBER (the derivative's value at one point); `sym_diff` gives you a new EXPRESSION (the derivative as a formula you can still evaluate anywhere, print, or differentiate again). Expressions live in a flat `Vec<ExprNode>` arena addressed by `i64` index rather than as a recursive struct/enum -- a deliberate workaround for v1's lack of self-referential types, not a stylistic choice (see the README's "Encoding" section for why a naive recursive `enum Expr` doesn't compile). Despite what the README's "What this library does NOT provide (yet)" section currently claims ("Integration, equation solving" as unimplemented "later phases"), this package (per its function list) actually already includes `sym_integrate`, `sym_solve_equation_le2`, `poly_factor_rational`, and `sym_factor_rational` -- reach for those directly rather than assuming you need to wait for a future version.

A single running expression, \(f(x) = x^2 + 3x\), threads through several of the notes below -- built once, then evaluated, differentiated, and solved, so you can watch one concrete expression move through the whole pipeline instead of a fresh example each time.

sym_add.intuition: Building an expression tree works one small piece at a time, like assembling a sentence from words -- `sym_add` doesn't compute anything, it just creates a new tree node that REMEMBERS "this position means: add whatever's at these two other positions." No arithmetic happens until something later (`sym_eval`) actually walks the tree.
sym_add.formula: Creates an `Add(a, b)` node representing \( a+b \).
sym_add.example: Building the running example \(f(x)=x^2+3x\), the LAST step is `sym_add(arena, idx_of_x_squared, idx_of_3x)` -- assuming \(x^2\) was already built at arena index 2 and \(3x\) at index 4, this call creates a new node at index 5 that says "add whatever's at index 2 and whatever's at index 4" -- it does NOT compute \(4+6=10\) or anything else yet, even if \(x\)'s value were already known.
sym_add.why: Keeping construction and evaluation completely separate is what makes the SAME built expression reusable -- evaluate it at \(x=2\), then again at \(x=5\), without rebuilding anything, since the tree itself never changes.

sym_sub.intuition: The same tree-construction idea as `sym_add`, for subtraction.
sym_sub.formula: Creates a `Sub(a, b)` node representing \( a-b \).
sym_sub.example: `sym_sub(arena, a, b)` where `a` points at a node for \(5\) and `b` points at a node for \(2\) creates a new `Sub` node -- evaluating it later (via `sym_eval`) produces \(3\), but building it doesn't compute anything yet, same as `sym_add`.
sym_sub.why: Kept as its own node kind (rather than desugaring to \(a+(-b)\) the way [vani-bignum](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-bignum)'s `bn_sub` does internally) so that printing the expression back out (`sym_to_str`) shows the subtraction the way you actually wrote it, `5 - 2`, not `5 + -2`.

sym_mul.formula: Creates a `Mul(a, b)` node representing \( a\times b \).
sym_mul.example: Building the running example's \(3x\) term: `sym_mul(arena, idx_of_3, idx_of_x)` creates a node meaning "multiply whatever's at the `3` node by whatever's at the `x` node" -- this is the node that later becomes \(6\) once \(x\) is evaluated at \(2\), but at construction time it's still just an unevaluated instruction.
sym_mul.why: `Mul` nodes are exactly what `sym_diff`'s product rule pattern-matches against -- differentiating an expression means walking the tree and dispatching on each node's KIND, so having a distinct `Mul` node (rather than, say, folding multiplication into a general N-ary node) is what makes the one-rule-per-kind design in `sym_diff` possible.

sym_div.formula: Creates a `Div(a, b)` node representing \( a/b \).
sym_div.example: `sym_div(arena, a, b)` where `a` is a node for \(10\) and `b` is a node for \(4\) builds a `Div` node -- `sym_eval` would compute \(10/4\), and since `sym_eval` works in `i64`, that's INTEGER division (\(2\), truncated), not \(2.5\) -- a real thing to watch for if you're used to expression evaluators that default to floating point.
sym_div.why: This is the node `sym_diff`'s quotient rule pattern-matches against -- see `sym_diff`'s own worked example for how a `Div` node's derivative gets built.

sym_pow.intuition: Same idea, for exponentiation -- but this is the one construction function whose EVALUATION has a real restriction worth knowing about upfront: only nonnegative integer exponents are supported when the tree is actually evaluated, even though the node itself can be built with any exponent subexpression.
sym_pow.example: Building the running example's \(x^2\) term: `sym_pow(arena, idx_of_x, idx_of_2)` creates a node meaning \(x^2\). If you instead built `sym_pow(arena, idx_of_x, idx_of_negative_1)` (representing \(x^{-1}\)), construction would still succeed -- the restriction only bites when `sym_eval` actually tries to walk that node and finds a negative exponent, at which point it traps.
sym_pow.why: This is exactly the exponent restriction `sym_diff`'s power rule also depends on: the rule \((u^n)'=n\,u^{n-1}u'\) requires \(n\) to be a literal `Num` node specifically (not an arbitrary subexpression), because differentiating with a VARIABLE exponent needs logarithmic differentiation, a different rule this package doesn't implement.

sym_neg.intuition: The one-argument counterpart to `sym_add`/`sym_sub`/etc. -- flips a value's sign.
sym_neg.example: `sym_neg(arena, idx_of_5)` creates a node meaning \(-5\) -- and `sym_neg` applied AGAIN to that result represents \(-(-5)\), which `sym_simplify` knows how to fold back down to plain \(5\) (one of its documented identities).
sym_neg.why: Having a dedicated unary `Neg` node (rather than desugaring negation to `Mul(-1, x)`) is what lets `sym_simplify`'s `Neg(Neg(x)) -> x` identity exist as a simple, direct pattern match, rather than needing to recognize `Mul(-1, Mul(-1, x))` as the same thing.

sym_eval.intuition: Walk the tree from the root down, and at every node, do what that node's KIND says: for a number, return it; for a variable, look up its current value; for an operator, evaluate both children first and then combine them. This is exactly how you'd evaluate a hand-written expression on paper -- work from the inside out.
sym_eval.formula: Recursively evaluate the subtree at `root`, substituting each `Var` node's value from `var_values[var_id]`; traps if a `Pow` node's exponent evaluates to negative.
sym_eval.example: Evaluate the running example \(f(x)=x^2+3x\) at \(x=2\) (so `var_values = [2]`, since \(x\) was interned as `var_id` 0). Walk the tree from the root (the `Add` node): its left child is the \(x^2\) subtree -- evaluate \(x\) as \(2\), then \(2^2=4\). Its right child is the \(3x\) subtree -- evaluate \(3\) as itself and \(x\) as \(2\), then \(3\times2=6\). Combine at the root: \(4+6=10\). So \(f(2)=10\) -- matching \(x^2+3x\) at \(x=2\) computed by hand: \(4+6=10\).
sym_eval.why: Evaluation is STRICT: both children of a binary node are always evaluated, even in a case where a smarter evaluator might skip one (e.g. \(0 \times \text{something\_that\_would\_trap}\) still evaluates the right side here) -- this is why `sym_simplify`'s \(0\times x \to 0\) identity genuinely changes behavior, not just presentation, whenever \(x\) itself would trap if evaluated: simplifying first can make an expression that used to trap evaluate cleanly instead.

sym_simplify.intuition: Raw expressions built directly (or produced by `sym_diff`) often contain obviously-reducible pieces -- multiplying by 1, adding 0, or several copies of the same variable term added together. `sym_simplify` walks the tree once and cleans up exactly these well-understood patterns, without attempting anything more ambitious like full polynomial factoring.
sym_simplify.formula: Constant folding + identities (\(x\cdot1\to x\), \(x\cdot0\to0\), \(x/1\to x\), \(x^1\to x\), \(x^0\to1\), \(-(-x)\to x\)) plus like-term collection across a flattened `Add`/`Sub` chain.
sym_simplify.example: Simplify \(2x+3x\) (a fresh small example, separate from the running \(f\), chosen because \(f\) itself has no like terms to collect): both terms are single-variable monomials with the SAME variable \(x\), so the like-term collector merges their coefficients: \(2+3=5\), giving \(5x\). Now try \(x-x\): same variable, coefficients \(1\) and \(-1\), which cancel to \(0\): the result is the literal `Num(0)`, not an unevaluated `Sub` node.
sym_simplify.why: This is DELIBERATELY not full polynomial normal form -- \(2\times(3\times x)\) does NOT fold to \(6x\) here, because that needs multiplicative-factor combination this pass doesn't attempt (see the README's "Simplification scope" for the exact boundary). Know this limit before assuming `sym_simplify` will fully canonicalize an arbitrary expression.

sym_diff.intuition: Differentiation is a set of mechanical rewrite rules, one per kind of expression -- a sum differentiates by differentiating each half and adding the results, a product needs the product rule, and so on. `sym_diff` applies exactly this: it walks the tree and, at each node, dispatches on that node's KIND to decide which rule applies, building a NEW expression that represents the derivative.
sym_diff.formula: \( \frac{d}{dx}c=0 \), \( \frac{d}{dx}x=1 \) (else 0), \( (u+v)'=u'+v' \), \( (u-v)'=u'-v' \), \( (-u)'=-u' \), \( (uv)'=u'v+uv' \) (product rule), \( (u/v)'=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2} \) (quotient rule), \( (u^n)'=n\,u^{n-1}u' \) (power + chain rule, \(n\) a literal).
sym_diff.example: Differentiate the running example \(f(x)=x^2+3x\) with respect to \(x\). The root is an `Add(u,v)` node with \(u=x^2\), \(v=3x\), so the rule is \((u+v)'=u'+v'\) -- differentiate each side separately. For \(u=x^2\) (a `Pow` node, base \(x\), exponent literal \(2\)): the power rule gives \(u' = 2\cdot x^{2-1}\cdot(dx/dx) = 2\cdot x^1 \cdot 1\) -- note this raw output literally contains \(x^1\) and a multiplication by \(1\), not yet simplified. For \(v=3x\) (a `Mul` node, \(u_v=3\), \(v_v=x\)): the product rule gives \(v' = 0\cdot x + 3\cdot 1\) (since \(d/dx(3)=0\) and \(d/dx(x)=1\)). Combining: \(f'(x) = (2\cdot x^1\cdot1) + (0\cdot x + 3)\) -- exactly what calculus says \(f'(x)=2x+3\) should look like, just not yet folded down. Pipe this through `sym_simplify` to actually get the clean \(2x+3\): \(x^1\to x\), \(\cdot1\) drops out, \(0\cdot x\to0\), and the leftover \(2x + 0 + 3\) collects to \(2x+3\).
sym_diff.why: The raw, unsimplified output is a deliberate design choice, not an oversight -- `sym_diff` and `sym_simplify` are two separate, independently testable passes, so a bug in simplification can never accidentally hide a bug in a differentiation rule (and vice versa). Always pipe `sym_diff`'s output through `sym_simplify` before printing it for a human to read.

sym_poly_coeffs_le2.intuition: Once an expression is a simple polynomial in one variable, it's often more useful as a plain list of coefficients (which a numeric solver can consume directly) than as a tree. This function bridges the two representations for the common, simple case of quadratic-or-lower expressions.
sym_poly_coeffs_le2.formula: Extracts \((c_0, c_1, c_2)\) from an expression matching \(c_0 + c_1x + c_2x^2\), by flattening the same `Add`/`Sub` chain `sym_simplify`'s like-term collector already knows how to walk.
sym_poly_coeffs_le2.example: Extract coefficients from the running example \(f(x)=x^2+3x\): matching against \(c_0+c_1x+c_2x^2\), there's no constant term (\(c_0=0\)), the linear term's coefficient is \(3\) (\(c_1=3\)), and the quadratic term's coefficient is \(1\) (\(c_2=1\), from the bare \(x^2\) with an implicit coefficient of 1). Result: \((0,3,1)\).
sym_poly_coeffs_le2.why: This coefficient triple is exactly the shape [vani-algebra](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-algebra)'s quadratic-solving machinery (and the compiler's own `f64_quadratic_root` builtin) expects -- extraction here is what lets `sym_solve_poly_le2` hand off to a NUMERIC solver instead of needing its own symbolic solving logic.

sym_solve_poly_le2.intuition: Once you have a polynomial's coefficients (via `sym_poly_coeffs_le2`), solving \(p(x)=0\) is a numeric problem this package doesn't need to solve itself -- it can just hand the coefficients to a numeric root-finder someone else already built and tested.
sym_solve_poly_le2.formula: Extracts coefficients via `sym_poly_coeffs_le2`, then solves using the compiler's `f64_quadratic_root` builtin (for the quadratic case).
sym_solve_poly_le2.example: Solve the running example's \(f(x)=x^2+3x=0\). From `sym_poly_coeffs_le2`'s example, the coefficients are \((c_0,c_1,c_2)=(0,3,1)\), i.e. \(x^2+3x+0=0\). Factor by hand to check: \(x(x+3)=0\), giving roots \(x=0\) and \(x=-3\) -- and indeed the quadratic formula on \(a=1,b=3,c=0\) gives \(x=\dfrac{-3\pm\sqrt{9-0}}{2}=\dfrac{-3\pm3}{2}\), which is \(0\) or \(-3\), matching.
sym_solve_poly_le2.why: This function is symbolic EXTRACTION feeding a NUMERIC solve, not a symbolic solution -- the roots come back as plain `f64` values, not as new expression-tree nodes you could differentiate or manipulate further.

sym_solve_equation_le2.intuition: An equation like \(\text{lhs}=\text{rhs}\) (two separate expressions, not yet combined) is the same problem as \(\text{lhs}-\text{rhs}=0\) (one expression set equal to zero) -- so this function's first move is just to rewrite the equation into that single-expression shape, then reuse `sym_solve_poly_le2` on the result.
sym_solve_equation_le2.formula: Rewrites \(\text{lhs}=\text{rhs}\) as \(\text{lhs}-\text{rhs}=0\), then applies the same degree-\(\le2\) polynomial solve as `sym_solve_poly_le2`.
sym_solve_equation_le2.example: Solve \(x^2+3x = 4\) (the running example's \(f(x)\), set equal to \(4\) instead of \(0\)). Rewrite: \((x^2+3x) - 4 = 0\), i.e. \(x^2+3x-4=0\). Factor to check: \((x+4)(x-1)=x^2+3x-4\) -- confirmed by expanding. Roots: \(x=-4\) and \(x=1\).
sym_solve_equation_le2.why: This lets you pose a problem in the NATURAL two-sided form (\(x^2+3x=4\)) rather than requiring the caller to manually rearrange every equation into `expression = 0` form before calling a solver -- the rearrangement is mechanical, so the function does it for you.
